passage: I'm Vidya, and I share Room 214 in the hostel with Ayesha. This term she has lived on late-night chai and videos in bed, then slept through her morning lectures. Last week she snapped at me for asking about the laundry, then sat on her bed staring at nothing. On Friday she said, "I just feel flat. Maybe I need a new study app, or one of those morning-routine videos." I didn't know what was going on inside her, so I only said, "You've barely slept all week." She looked surprised, as if she hadn't connected the two. Since Sunday she has set one alarm for the same time every day and put the kettle away at night. She's laughing at my jokes again, though I can't say for sure that's why.

Week three: Ojas found her half asleep in the library. "You're not lazy, you're exhausted. Try one thing: the same wake-up every day, even Sunday." Jahnavi grumbled but set the alarm.

Warden's log, Block C, Thursday
Kalyani from room 214 has been in the common room past two most nights this month, laptop open, chai flask beside her. Her roommate says she misses the nine o'clock lecture twice a week. Today she snapped at the mess staff over cold rice, then sat on the stairs looking flat rather than angry. I asked if she was all right. She said she felt anxious all the time and didn't know why; she thought she just needed more motivation. I asked when she last slept a full night. She laughed, then stopped laughing. We agreed on a small trial: lights off by 12:30 for one week, chai only before five, and a walk to breakfast. I'll check in with her on Monday.
Yusuf

passage:
Sunday night
Weird week. Monday to Thursday I was up till three finishing the fest posters, living on chai from the gate stall. Skipped two labs. On Friday I cried because Tanuja borrowed my charger without asking. Over a charger! Then I felt nothing at all for a whole day, like someone had turned my colour down.
Today I slept eleven hours by accident and woke up fine. Happy, even. Tanuja pointed out, gently, that I'm always "dramatic" on Fridays, after the late nights. Rude but true.
So, an experiment. Bed by 12:30 on weeknights, phone on the other side of the room, no chai after dinner. Not a new planner, not another productivity video. Just sleep. Let's see if Friday Keerthana is nicer.

qa.a: The fest posters.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling on Friday after the charger incident?
qa.a: Keerthana felt upset, then flat and empty for a whole day, as if someone had turned the colour down.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana's experiment work better than a new planner?
qa.a: Regular sleep deals with the real cause of the Friday moods, so a small routine change can lift mood more than a motivation trick.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt when Keerthana cried over the charger?
qa.a: Tanuja may have been startled and hurt, yet later pointed out the Friday pattern gently.

grounding: Shows a college student whose late nights, chai and skipped labs leave them teary and flat, and who tries small regular sleep changes instead of a motivation trick.

passage: At the agricultural college hostel outside Dharwad, Parul's nights ran on chai from the gate stall and chats until three. She slept through the eight o'clock lecture twice a week and felt flat all afternoon. On Thursday she cried because a senior didn't reply to her message, and on Friday she shouted at Bhupen for borrowing her notes. 'What's wrong with me? Maybe I need a new timetable app,' she groaned. Bhupen, from the next village, grinned. 'Maybe you need sleep. Try lights off by midnight for one week. No chai after dinner.' Grumbling, she tried it. By the next Thursday she made the eight o'clock lecture and laughed at Bhupen's jokes again.
